children.text: In Lazi town in southeastern Siquijor, a church completed in 1884 from coral stone and timber faces one of the largest old conventos in the Philippines across the road. Explore the church with its intact wooden floor and the museum inside the convento, and pair the visit with nearby Cambugahay Falls.

Lazi Church, officially San Isidro Labrador Parish Church, is a coral-stone church in the heart of Lazi town in southeastern Siquijor, right beside the island's ring road. Across the road a huge two-story convento faces the church, and together the pair preserves the look of a Spanish colonial town center. It lies only about
2km
from Cambugahay Falls, the island's most popular attraction, so many travelers stop by on the way to the falls, and it is regarded as Siquijor's signature heritage site.
Lazi, formerly called Tigbawan, became a parish independent of Siquijor on
August 8, 1857
. Under the direction of Augustinian Recollect priest Father Toribio Sánchez, Filipino artisans built the church from coral stone quarried from the sea and hardwood, completing it in
and raising the bell tower the following year. The convento across the road was begun in
and blessed in
. A convento is the Spanish-era rectory and friary built beside a church; it is sometimes rendered as "nunnery" because of the English word convent, but this one housed Recollect priests.
By presidential decree the church and convento were declared National Historical Landmarks, and a national historical marker was installed in
; in
the National Museum declared them a National Cultural Treasure. Since

the church has also been on the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List under "Baroque Churches of the Philippines (Extension)," together with the churches of Boljoon, Guiuan, Loboc and Tumauini. It is not yet an inscribed World Heritage Site, so take claims of "UNESCO World Heritage" with a grain of salt. In
the National Historical Commission restored the church at a cost of about
and handed it back to the diocese.
The site is compact, and
30 minutes–1 hour

is plenty to see both the church and the convento. Most visitors therefore fold it into a loop of the island's southeast with Cambugahay Falls and the century-old balete tree. It suits travelers interested in old architecture and history, as well as families looking for a shady place to rest after swimming at the falls. It is still an active parish where Mass is held, so visit quietly and respectfully.

blocks.title: Coral-stone facade and three-level bell tower

children.text: The facade is built of coral-stone blocks quarried from the sea, with only the pediment in wood, and a three-level bell tower topped with a red dome stands on its south side. The main door faces northeast, so the stone texture looks best in the morning sun.

The entire nave is covered with a hardwood floor (entarimado) laid in a zigzag pattern whose points aim toward the altar and the main door. Few churches in the Philippines keep an old wooden floor this intact, making it the church's greatest pride.

Five retablos survive, including the gilded main retablo (altarpiece) behind the high altar, along with two pulpits. Look up as well at the ceiling painted with vine motifs on a blue ground and at the colored glass windows.
The convento across the road is a U-shaped two-story building measuring about

, with coral-stone arches and walls on the ground floor and timber construction above. The national marker calls it one of the largest conventos in the Philippines, and locals sometimes introduce it as "the largest and oldest convent in Asia."

blocks.title: Convento upper floor and Siquijor Heritage Museum

children.text: The convento houses the Siquijor Heritage Museum, which displays old statues of saints, vestments, church artifacts, old photographs and furniture. The spacious sala and dining area, hardwood floors and large wooden windows set with colored glass hint at life in a 19th-century rectory.

On the church wall is a national historical marker framed with pieces of coral. Written in Filipino, it records the Recollects' founding of the parish, the construction dates of the church and convento, and the convento's dimensions, so a photo of it is handy during your visit.

blocks.title: Strolling the grounds under old acacias

children.text: Century-old acacia (rain tree) trees spread wide shade around the church and convento. From the lawn you can fit both buildings in one frame, and it is a pleasant spot to rest after a swim at the falls.

This route sweeps the island's southeast in one go, so it works best on a motorbike or a tricycle hired for the day. Many stretches of the ring road have few streetlights at night, so head back before dark.
Flights from Manila to Dumaguete-Sibulan Airport (DGT) take about
1 hour 20 minutes
. From the airport to Dumaguete port is about
15–20 minutes
by tricycle or taxi, and from the port you take a boat to Siquijor.
Since
December 2025
, Sunlight Air has flown direct between Cebu and Siquijor (about
55 minutes
) a few times a week. From Siquijor Airport to Lazi takes about
45–60 minutes
by tricycle; flight days change often, so check the airline's announcements.

The ring road is well paved with light traffic and easy to ride, but you need a license (an international permit is accepted) and a helmet. You can park motorbikes along the road in front of the church and on the open lot opposite.
Day tours from Dumaguete that combine the boat crossing and an island loop almost always include Lazi Church and the convento. They are reported to cost about
per person, but time at the church tends to be short, so stay a night on the island if you want to see the museum at leisure. Check the latest details of what is included with the tour operator.
Siquijor's dry season runs
November–May
, when boats are reliable and the island is easy to tour by motorbike, making it the best time to visit the church as well. Within that period,
November–January
is relatively cool, while in
March–May

midday is very hot and the shadeless grounds and the convento's upper floor heat up, so go in the morning or late afternoon. The church and convento are indoors, so they are good to visit on rainy days too.
June–October

is the rainy season, with frequent afternoon showers; when typhoon or gale warnings are raised, boats to and from Dumaguete may be canceled, so allow a spare day. The feast of Lazi's patron saint, San Isidro Labrador, falls on
May 15
, when the church holds a feast-day Mass and the town celebrates, so expect crowds. During Holy Week, domestic travelers flock to the island, so book boats and lodging early.

Lazi is a quiet rural town gathered around its church, market and government offices, so lodging options are few. Most travelers stay on the San Juan coast in the island's southwest, where restaurants and dive shops cluster, and ride about
30 minutes
to Lazi. In San Juan, fan rooms with shared bathrooms cost about
a night, guesthouses with air-conditioning and private bathrooms about
, and beachfront mid-range resorts about
. If you want to reach the falls early, you can also stay at a small resort in Lazi or on the neighboring Maria coast.

Lazi town has carinderias (eateries where you pick dishes from a display to eat with rice), bakeries and market stalls, good for a simple lunch. Grilled fish, kinilaw (raw fish cured in vinegar) and seafood cooked in coconut milk are everyday fare in Siquijor's coastal villages; for Western-style cafés and more varied restaurants, head back to San Juan for dinner. There are no snack stands inside the church or convento, so bring water.
The church is usually open during the day, and the convento museum is reported to open around
. No official hours are posted, so go in the morning rather than late afternoon.
Wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees. If you are coming straight from the falls, bring a shirt or shawl to throw over your wet swimsuit.
Masses on Sunday mornings and on weekday early mornings and late afternoons may limit visits inside the church. Check the latest Mass times on the parish notice board or locally.
Photography is sometimes not allowed inside the convento museum. Ask the caretaker before taking pictures.
The main door faces northeast, so morning is best for photos of the facade. To fit both the church and the convento in one frame, step back onto the lawn beside the church.
The museum fee, donations and transport on the island are paid in cash. Bring plenty of coins and small bills.
Tour groups crowd Cambugahay Falls after
. Go to the falls first and see the church afterward to enjoy both while they are quiet.
Reading a little about the Spanish-era Recollect missions and the history of Siquijor before your visit makes the marker and the exhibits far more rewarding.
The church is still an active parish where Masses, weddings and funerals are held. During services, do not walk inside or use flash, and keep your voice down.
The wooden floor, walls and statues are part of a National Cultural Treasure. Do not touch or lean on them, and take care not to scratch the floor with high heels or shoes covered in wet sand.
The old wooden stairs and floors on the convento's upper level can be slippery or creaky. Hold children's hands and do not enter rooms or areas that are closed off.
Always wear a helmet when riding a motorbike, and watch for dogs, livestock and speed bumps in front of villages on the ring road. Many stretches have few streetlights at night.
If someone offers to act as your guide, agree on the fee first. It is safest to pay the museum fee or donation directly at the official counter or box.
Boats can be canceled suddenly during the rainy and typhoon seasons. Do not plan a tight schedule on the day you leave the island, and check the shipping line's latest announcements.

An island you can circle in a day on a ring road of about
72km
. Covers the whole island, from San Juan's sunset beaches and caves to its traditional healing culture.
The most common gateway city to Siquijor, about
45 minutes–2 hours
away by boat. With an airport, hotels and restaurants, it is a good place to spend a night before or after visiting the island.
